literature.short:
Good morning, Yamuna. Today's literary news has a fine mix of painters' eyes, poets' voices and some very large books, so let me begin with the seeing.

The Guardian marks the centenary of John Berger with a "where to start" guide to his work. It introduces a writer who moved freely between genres, writing about art, love and mortality, and it makes a good map if you want to return to his essays on painting and looking. Also in the Guardian, there is an exhibition devoted to Jan Potocki's The Manuscript Found in Saragossa, the surreal Enlightenment novel with a famously strange origin story. The paper's headline asks whether one of the great novels of the Enlightenment was written by a man who thought he was a werewolf, which tells you the tone. The curators argue that its global humanism feels pertinent today, and its wandering, unreliable narrator sounds like a perfect companion for a long evening. Over at Literary Hub, Priyanka Kumar writes about bringing art into her nature writing. She starts from a snowy encounter with a coyote near her home, and she explains her idea of the microwild, a way of attending to the wildness found close by. It is a thoughtful piece on how visual art and the writing of place can feed one another.

Now to the prizes, which have been busy. China Miéville has won the Goldsmiths prize, worth ten thousand pounds, for The Rouse. The Guardian describes it as a blend of paranormal thriller and historical saga, running to one thousand two hundred and sixty-four pages and spanning British imperial and Cold War history. It took him two decades to write. The judges called it exuberant and overflowing, and one said he was destined for this award. In non-fiction, Edmund Richardson has won the fifty-thousand-pound Baillie Gifford prize for Alexander: God, King, Man. The Guardian's reviewer calls it a dazzling, dizzying adventure, a riveting account of Alexander's early reign that reads history as a vivid, narrative journey. And on the Booker, a critic at The i Paper says they have read every novel on this year's shortlist and believes there is a clear winner. It is a nice opportunity to see how someone argues a case across the whole list. Literary Hub also reports that the American Library in Paris has named the winner of its 2026 Book Award, which honours fiction and nonfiction drawing on France as a timeless source of inspiration. The winner is Hotel Exile: Paris.

On the subject of immersive fiction, the Guardian reviews Min Jin Lee's American Hagwon, the third book in her Diaspora Quartet and a follow-up to Pachinko. It follows a Korean family whose devotion to their children's education drives the story, and the review praises it as gloriously immersive and led by character, which is just what made Pachinko so absorbing.

Turning to poetry and the pleasure of language, Literary Hub has printed Mahmoud Darwish's poem "Arabic Music" in full. It is meditative, built on questions about stones, clouds and sparrows, and it is the kind of poem that asks to be read aloud. The Guardian has an interview with the Indian-Irish poet Nikita Gill, who talks about her earliest reading memories at sea with her sailor father. She speaks of the Mahabharata retelling that inspired her to write, and of her admiration for Arundhati Roy and Lucille Clifton. Her title says it all: she read Flowers in the Attic too young, and feels someone should have stopped her. Also at Literary Hub, Hanif Abdurraqib writes about teaching high school writers in Columbus, Ohio, and what he has learned from the poet June Jordan. It is an essay about poetry, teaching and how writers are made, and I suspect it may strike a chord from your own classroom.

Two short pieces of fiction at Literary Hub are worth a few quiet minutes. "Remember the Bees" is a brief opening passage set on red earth under an early, lingering heat, with a grandfather at its centre, and its pleasure is in the sensory, unhurried narration. "Dams" is an excerpt in which a character named Ada, over coffee, notices the translucence of the words escriure and novel·la as she explains why she has come back. It is attentive, lyrical prose, with a close eye on words themselves, and it may especially appeal to someone who lives between languages.

Finally, a few pieces that tie writing to history and place. Literary Hub carries an essay on Alan Moore's V for Vendetta as a dystopia for our times. It opens in the medieval undercroft beneath the Palace of Westminster, and it considers the work as both a historical engagement and a piece of craft. And there is an extract from Monica Nelson's These Long Shadows, taking us inside Eudora Welty's house in Jackson, Mississippi, which is now open to the public. It looks closely at a writer's home and its place in Southern literary history, and it is a pleasing thing to read if you enjoy seeing where a voice came from.

That is all for today, and I hope one of these finds its way into your evening, perhaps with a cup of something warm.
literature.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's a rich couple of days in the reading world, with a centenary, a few big prizes, and some lovely pieces about the sound and sight of language.

Let me begin with seeing, since several of today's pieces circle around painting and attention. The Guardian has published a "where to start" guide to John Berger, marking a hundred years since his birth. It's a useful map of a writer who refused to stay in one box. His work moves between essays, fiction and more, and keeps returning to art, love and mortality. For someone who likes to set a painting beside a page of prose, he is a natural companion, because his essays on painting are really essays on how we look. The guide is meant for newcomers, so it could be a handy thing to pass on to a curious sixth-former as well as to read yourself.

In a similar spirit, Literary Hub has Priyanka Kumar on how she brings art into her nature writing. She starts from a snowy encounter with a coyote near her home, and she talks about an idea of hers that she calls the microwild. It's a thoughtful piece about how looking at images changes the way you write a place, and how a small, close encounter can hold a whole landscape. Given that you live up in Belledonne, with the valley below and the weather changing the view all the time, I suspect the idea of a microwild will feel familiar. It may well send you out for a walk before it sends you to a bookshop.

Now to the big, ambitious books, and the prizes that have been going to them. The headline in The Guardian is that China Miéville has won the Goldsmiths prize, worth ten thousand pounds, for The Rouse. It's a novel of one thousand two hundred and sixty-four pages, and it blends paranormal thriller with historical saga, running through British imperial history and into the Cold War. It took him two decades to write. The judges called it exuberant and overflowing, and one of them said he was "destined for this award". There's something rather joyful about a prize going to a book that so openly refuses to be tidy. The combination of a thriller's pull with a long historical sweep is, I think, close to the sort of novel you enjoy: one where history comes in through story rather than through footnotes.

Another prize, in the world of narrative history: The Guardian reviews Edmund Richardson's Alexander: God, King, Man, which has just won the Baillie Gifford prize, worth fifty thousand pounds. The reviewer calls it a dazzling, dizzying adventure, and a riveting account of Alexander's early reign. The point of interest for you is probably the way it treats history as adventure, with a vivid, driving narrative rather than a dry chronicle. It's a reminder that the line between the novelist's craft and the historian's can be rather thin when the writing is good.

Staying with large stories and prizes, there's the Booker. A reviewer at The i Paper says they have read every novel on this year's shortlist, and argues that there is a clear winner. I can't tell you from the summary which book they choose, but the exercise itself is appealing: a single reader working through the whole shortlist and then committing to a verdict. If you've been following the shortlist, it might be fun to read it with your own favourite in mind and see whether you agree.

And there's one more award for anyone with a soft spot for Paris. The American Library in Paris has named the winner of its 2026 Book Award, which honours fiction and nonfiction that draw on France as a timeless source of inspiration. The winner is Hotel Exile: Paris. The title alone suggests a story about displacement and the city as refuge. It's a nice category of prize, because it's about the relationship between a place and the people who write about it.

Speaking of novels with a sense of lives lived across places, The Guardian has a review of American Hagwon, by Min Jin Lee. It's the third book in her Diaspora Quartet and a follow-up to Pachinko. It follows a Korean family whose devotion to their children's education drives the story. The reviewer calls it gloriously immersive, and praises the way it is led by character. That is exactly the quality that makes Pachinko such a good book for stepping into a world you don't already know. You don't need to be familiar with the culture first, because the family carries you in. And since you teach, the theme of a family organised around education may have a particular resonance.

Next, an unusual one, and it's a delight. The Guardian asks whether one of the great novels of the Enlightenment was written by a man who thought he was a werewolf. The novel is The Manuscript Found in Saragossa, by Jan Potocki, a surreal book with a famously strange origin story. There's an exhibition about it at the moment, and the curators argue that its global humanism feels relevant now. It has a wandering, unreliable narrator, and stories that nest inside other stories, which is the kind of storytelling that rewards a reader who enjoys being led astray. For a classroom, a novel with a story as odd as its pages might be a good way into the idea that fiction is made, not just found.

Now for the pieces that are really about language itself, which I suspect you'll like best. Literary Hub has published three short things you could read aloud.

The first is the opening of a piece of fiction called "Remember the Bees". It begins on red earth, under an early heat that lingers, and the focus is a grandfather. The excerpt is brief, but it's immersive and sensory, and written in a quiet prose that lets the setting do the work. It's the kind of opening that makes you want to know who the grandfather is before you know anything else.

The second is an excerpt from a story called "Dams". Over coffee, a woman called Ada explains why she has returned, and in the middle of it she notices the translucence of two words: escriure, to write, and novel·la, novel. It's a lovely moment, where a character looks at words as though they were glass. For someone who teaches in two languages, and lives among several, I think that attention to how a word looks and feels will land very well.

And the third is a poem by Mahmoud Darwish, printed in full: "Arabic Music". It's a meditative piece, full of questions about stones, clouds and sparrows. It has the musicality that you enjoy, and it's one of those poems that asks to be read slowly, and aloud, rather than analysed. If you wanted a short text to bring into a lesson on how sound carries meaning, this would be a gentle candidate, though I'd read it yourself first and let it sit.

On the subject of poets, The Guardian has an interview with Nikita Gill, the Indian-Irish poet, under the headline "I read Flowers in the Attic too young. Someone should have stopped me." It's a personal conversation about reading and how a poet is made. She talks about her earliest reading memories, which were at sea with her father, who was a sailor. She also mentions a retelling of the Mahabharata that inspired her to start writing, and she says she admires Arundhati Roy and Lucille Clifton. It's a nice thing to read for the picture of a child growing up among books on ships, and for the way she traces her own writing back to one story she loved.

There's a companion piece on Literary Hub, in which Hanif Abdurraqib writes about teaching high school writers in Columbus, Ohio, and what he has learned from the poet June Jordan. It's an essay about poetry, teaching, and how writers are formed. Since you spend your days with teenagers and texts, I think you'll recognise something in it, perhaps the way a teacher can learn as much from a poet as from a class. It's an essay about the work of passing on a love of writing, and it's honest about how that happens.

Finally, two pieces that tie literature to place and history. Literary Hub has an essay on Alan Moore's V for Vendetta, called "A Dystopia For Our Times". It opens with the medieval undercroft beneath the Palace of Westminster, and from that old stone it moves into the work itself. The opening is a clever move, because it roots a comic about the future in a very old British building, and it suggests that the history is part of the machinery of the story. It could be an interesting way into a discussion of how dystopias use real places.

And lastly, an extract from Monica Nelson's book These Long Shadows, about Eudora Welty's house in Jackson, Mississippi, which is now open to the public. It looks closely at a writer's home and what it says about her place in Southern literary history. Writers' houses are always a bit of a pilgrimage, and this one invites you to think about how a life in one town and one house could feed so much fiction. It's an agreeable note to end on, since it's about the quiet rooms where books begin.

That's the Literature briefing for today, and I hope there's something here to read slowly with your coffee.

art.short:
Good morning, Yamuna. Here is your art briefing for the last two days, with a good deal happening close to home this weekend and a few stories worth stepping into further afield.

Let me begin in Grenoble, where Saturday is busy at the Musée de Grenoble. The museum is showing sculptures and paintings by the American artist Anne Truitt. The listing I found is very short and gives no dates, so it is worth checking the museum's own pages before you go, but it is a name to put in the diary. Also on Saturday, at half past two in the afternoon, there is an event called "Le dernier passage", open to all audiences. The listing doesn't say what it focuses on, so consider it a small mystery. At half past four there is a guided tour of the François Morellet display, titled "Sous la géométrie, la facétie", which means "Under the geometry, the mischief". Morellet's playful, geometric abstraction is a lovely way in for anyone who thinks abstraction is cold, because the humour is part of the point. Yesterday, at lunchtime, the museum also hosted "Ballade Européenne", a concert with an Irish programme, part of its Musée en musique series. That has now passed, but it suggests the series may bring more midday music.

Also on Saturday, the seventh of November, Le Mois de la Photo has an event at the Ancien musée de Peinture in Grenoble. Unidivers gives few details, but it is close to home and timely. And in Isère, Lyon Capitale reports on eight poetry evenings, "à l'écoute de notre planète", listening to our planet, at the Musée de la Résistance et de la Déportation. No dates are given in the text, but poetry in a museum of memory sounds like your sort of evening.

Now to Lyon, where Le Petit Bulletin has a piece I rather liked. It looks at a comic book about the women drivers, nurses and rescuers who served in military emergency units, tied to an exhibition at the CHRD. The story centres on Madeleine Pauliac, a military doctor, and the people she describes as an angle mort of history, a blind spot. It is history recovered through graphic storytelling, which could be a nice thing to show a class. Looking ahead, the Fête des lumières returns to Lyon from the fifth to the eighth of December. It is the twenty-seventh edition, with twenty-seven works, a route that comes back to place Bellecour, and some installations built on artificial intelligence or designed to be interactive. It is a little later than the immediate weeks, but easy to reach from Grenoble if you fancy planning ahead.

A little south, in the Drôme, ici.fr reports that shoes from the Musée de la chaussure in Romans are taking up residence at the château de Grignan. I only have the headline, which asks why, so I can't tell you the reason. But a shoe collection in a historic château is an intriguing pairing, and Grignan, of course, has its own literary associations.

On to the stories that read like fiction. Beaux Arts Magazine looks at an exhibition at the château de Chantilly about the pink diamond, a jewel stolen in 1926, later recovered, and wrapped in legend ever since. The magazine's headline calls it a "miraculé", a miraculous survivor. Theft, disappearance, rediscovery and mystery all in one stone: it has the shape of a novel. Also from Beaux Arts, the Bibliothèque nationale de France in Paris is celebrating the obsessions of Georges Perec, with an exhibition drawing on more than forty years of his work across literature and the visual arts. It is described as teeming and wide-ranging, and given Perec's love of lists, puzzles and constraints, that seems exactly right. For someone who enjoys the meeting point of word and image, it looks like a rich one.

Now beyond France, and first to Scotland. The Guardian looks at a new exhibition on Roman Scotland, and the headline asks what the Romans ever gave the Scots. The answer, it seems, is heated floors, flashy sandals, sun gods and a lot of nails. The show draws on finds such as altars to the sun god Sol and surviving leather shoes, including a discovery at Inveresk, near Edinburgh. There is something very moving about history told through a worn shoe, and it is much the same instinct as a good historical novel.

The Guardian also has a roundup of four free exhibitions, and two stand out. One features Sturtevant, whose forgeries of Warhol test your eye for real against fake. The other is Cady Noland, whose work offers a sharp critique of American culture. Questions of authorship and originality run through both, and they would make a good prompt for discussion.

On the radio, BBC Radio 4's Front Row speaks with the artist Sam Taylor-Johnson about portraiture and selfhood, as her new monograph appears. The conversation about how a portrait is actually made is the strongest part for an art lover. The same programme also hears from the film-maker Sian Heder, who discusses "Being Heumann" and the Disability Rights Movement.

Finally, a thoughtful question from London. The National Gallery has released a video about NG Citizens, an assembly of fifty people chosen by lottery to consider how the Gallery should connect people and paintings. It asks, quite simply, what a national collection should mean to the people it belongs to, and it is a gentle, interesting question to carry around the next time you stand in front of a painting.

Enjoy the weekend's galleries, Yamuna, and may Morellet's mischief put a smile on your Saturday.
art.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's Friday the sixth of November, and this morning's art news has a pleasingly literary streak, with plenty happening in Grenoble this weekend before we travel a little further afield.

Let me start close to home, because Saturday is a busy day at the Musée de Grenoble. At half past two in the afternoon there is an event called "Le dernier passage", open to all audiences. I should be honest that the listing says very little, so I can't tell you what its focus is. The title has a rather mysterious, almost novelistic ring, and it may be worth a message to the museum if you are tempted. Then at half past four there is a guided tour of the François Morellet display, called "Sous la géométrie, la facétie", which means "Under the geometry, the mischief". I like that title very much. Morellet's playful geometric abstraction is a lovely way into the museum, because it suggests that rigour and humour can share the same canvas. It is the sort of tour that might leave you looking at ordinary lines and grids a little differently on the walk back to the tram.

The museum is also showing sculptures and paintings by Anne Truitt, according to a short listing from jds.fr. I'm afraid it gives no dates and no further detail, so I can't say how long it runs or what exactly is on the walls. But it is at the museum you would most want to visit, so it seems worth checking the opening times on the museum's own pages before you plan an afternoon.

Also on Saturday, the seventh of November, Unidivers lists an event at the Ancien musée de Peinture in Grenoble, as part of Le Mois de la Photo. Again, the text is brief, so I can't tell you what form it takes. But the Mois de la Photo is under way, and that old museum building is a handsome setting, so it may be worth a look if you are in town for the Morellet tour. You could, in fact, make a gentle day of it: photography in the morning, then the museum in the afternoon.

One thing you've just missed, but which sounds delightful: yesterday, Thursday the fifth, at half past twelve, the Musée de Grenoble held a lunchtime concert called "Ballade Européenne : l'Irlande", part of its Musée en musique series, with an Irish programme of classical and folk music. I mention it mainly so you know the series exists. A midday concert among the paintings is a lovely idea, and there may be another in the same series before long.

Another local item is more poetic. Lyon Capitale reports on eight poetry evenings in Isère, titled "à l'écoute de notre planète", "listening to our planet", at the Musée de la Résistance et de la Déportation. The article, as given to me, doesn't include the dates, so that is something to look up. But I like the pairing very much: poetry spoken aloud in a museum that holds memory and testimony, with the natural world as the theme. It feels like an evening that might stay with you.

Now to Lyon, and to a story that links neatly to the idea of history told through narrative. Le Petit Bulletin Grenoble has a feature on a comic book about women drivers, nurses and rescuers in military emergency units. It is connected to an exhibition at the CHRD, the history centre in Lyon, and it centres on the military doctor Madeleine Pauliac. The journalist's phrase is that they are telling "an angle mort de l'histoire", a blind spot of history. I find that a good description of what the best historical fiction does too. It goes to the places the textbook skips and gives them faces and voices. A graphic narrative can do this in a particularly direct way, since the reader sees these women at work, in their vehicles and on their rounds, rather than just being told that they existed. It might even be a useful thing to show older pupils, as an example of how the form of a story shapes the history it tells.

Further ahead in Lyon, though not immediate, the twenty-seventh Fête des lumières runs from the fifth to the eighth of December. Le Petit Bulletin reports that there will be twenty-seven works, a full route returning to place Bellecour, and some installations based on artificial intelligence or designed to be interactive. It is a little later than the weeks we're usually looking at, but it is easy to reach from Grenoble, and if you fancy a winter evening of light and wandering, it is worth marking in the diary now.

Not far from here either, in the Drôme, ici.fr asks why shoes from the Musée de la chaussure in Romans are taking up residence at the château de Grignan. The article explains the reason for the loan, but all I have is the headline, so I can't give you the answer. What appeals to me is the idea itself: everyday objects, made to be worn and walked in, set down in a historic château. Shoes can say a lot about the lives that wore them, and a château is a place where you might expect to find grand portraits rather than footwear. If you are heading that way, it might be a pleasant excursion.

That thought of objects telling stories leads me to the other items on history. The Guardian has a piece on a new exhibition about Roman Scotland, with the splendid headline asking what the Romans ever gave Scotland, and answering with heated floors, flashy sandals, sun gods and a lot of nails. The show draws on finds such as altars to the sun god Sol and surviving leather shoes, including a discovery at Inveresk, near Edinburgh. I enjoy that the story is told through such humble things. A leather shoe that has survived all those centuries makes a person feel suddenly present in a way a grand inscription rarely does. It is a very good example of history that comes alive through the small and the worn, much as a good novel finds the large events inside a single life. And I can't help noticing that we've now had shoes twice this morning, in Drôme and in Scotland.

Then there is a story from Chantilly, which has the feel of a thriller. Beaux Arts Magazine reports that the château de Chantilly is exploring the destiny of its pink diamond, described by the magazine as a "miraculé", a miraculous survivor. The jewel was stolen in 1926, was later recovered, and has been wrapped in legend ever since. Theft, disappearance, rediscovery and mystery: it has all the ingredients a novelist would want. I do not have more detail than that, so I won't guess at how the exhibition tells it, but as a story, it is hard to resist. It would make a rather good prompt for a creative writing exercise, too: give a class the bare facts of a stolen jewel and ask them to supply the narrator.

Next, a few items where words and images meet. In Paris, the Bibliothèque nationale de France is celebrating the obsessions of Georges Perec with what Beaux Arts Magazine calls a teeming, abundant exhibition. It draws on more than forty years of his work, across literature and the visual arts. I think this is the show for you, because it links writing and image in precisely the way you enjoy. The description suggests something rich and wide-ranging, a writer's preoccupations laid out for visitors to follow, rather than a tidy chronological tour. If you find yourself in Paris, it sounds like a place to spend a good long while.

On the radio, BBC Radio 4's Front Row has a conversation with the artist Sam Taylor-Johnson about portraiture and selfhood, as her new monograph appears. The question of how a portrait is made, and what it says about the person depicted and the person making it, is fascinating, and it connects naturally with how narrators construct themselves in fiction. The same programme also features Sian Heder talking about "Being Heumann" and the Disability Rights Movement. It is a programme worth putting on while you cook.

Still on the subject of looking carefully, The Guardian has a roundup of four free exhibitions, with a headline asking whether you can tell a real Warhol from a fake. The show that gives the piece its title features Sturtevant's forgeries of Warhol, which test the viewer's eye and raise the question of what authorship even means. The roundup also mentions Cady Noland's sharp critique of American culture. I like the Sturtevant idea in particular. It is rather like asking a student to tell an original voice from a skilful pastiche, and discovering that the answer is not as simple as it sounds.

Finally, a thoughtful video from the National Gallery in London, about something it calls NG Citizens. It is a citizens' assembly of fifty people, chosen by lottery, who are considering how the Gallery should connect people and paintings. The video asks what the National Gallery should mean to the people it belongs to. I find that a lovely question, and one that applies well beyond London. A national collection belongs to everyone, but how often does anyone ask them what they want from it? It is a small but interesting window into how a major museum is trying to listen.

So, to gather the threads: this weekend, the Musée de Grenoble offers the Morellet tour and "Le dernier passage" on Saturday, alongside the Anne Truitt show and the Mois de la Photo event at the Ancien musée de Peinture. Poetry evenings are coming in Isère, the CHRD in Lyon is telling a neglected story of women in military emergency units, and further off there are lights in Lyon in December, a stolen diamond in Chantilly, and Perec in Paris.

That's all for this morning, Yamuna, and I hope Saturday finds you wandering happily among the geometry and the mischief.

bfi.short:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's a Hamlet-heavy couple of days in the BFI corner, with a few other bits of Shakespeare, Dickens and Atwood alongside, so let me take them by theme.

Hamlet first, since it's on the twenty twenty-seven list and so much of the news clusters around it. The most substantial item is The Guardian's review of a new stage Hamlet. The headline calls it extraordinary, says it turns Shakespeare inside out with infinite jest, and adds, rather wonderfully, cuddly toys. I only have the headline, so I can't tell you how the toys are used. But "infinite jest" is Hamlet's own phrase about Yorick, so the review is clearly playing with the skull scene and with the idea of the play as both grief and game. That might make a lively starting point for première pupils: how can a production lean into the comic side of a tragedy without losing its weight?

Close to that, Country and Town House has a stage note on Hamlet: Hail to the Thief at the Barbican in London. Again I have only the headline, so no cast, no dates and no verdict. But the title suggests a production focused on theft and usurpation, which is Claudius's crime at the heart of the play. If you're looking for an angle on kingship and legitimacy, it's worth a glance.

On screen, The Hindu reviews a new Hamlet film starring Riz Ahmed, under the headline "finds method in this madness". That's a nod to Polonius's line about Hamlet's feigned madness, and it suggests the critic is reading the performance through that question: is the madness real, performed, or a bit of both? It could be handy for pupils comparing how a play on the page, on the stage and on film handles that ambiguity.

There are also a few productions further afield. The Nevada Theatre is staging Hamlet through the eighth of November, presented by TheUnion.com as a Hamlet for our time. That's only two days away, and it's not exactly around the corner from Les Adrets, but the framing is interesting: the idea that the play speaks to the present day is something your seconde pupils might be asked to argue for or against. BroadwayWorld also announces that Thinking Cap Theatre is presenting Hamlet. There are no dates or details in what I have, so treat it as a note that the play keeps being staged rather than something to plan around.

Then there's something more playful. Starburst Magazine has an interview with Dan Sturman and R.C. Staab about Space Hamlet, a science-fiction reworking of the play. The extract is thin, so I can't tell you much about how the story is transposed. Still, as a conversation starter about adaptation, it's a fun contrast to the more traditional readings, and pupils might enjoy guessing what a space setting would do to "to be or not to be".

And to round off the Hamlet cluster, the University of Utah has a piece titled "Why Hamlet still matters". Again only the headline reached me, but it's the sort of framing question that works for a first lesson or a terminale essay prompt.

Moving on to the rest of the programme. The review of Great Expectations at the Brockley Jack Studio in London comes from southlondon.co.uk. All I have is the title, so I can't report on the staging choices. But Dickens is on the twenty twenty-seven list, and small studio productions of the novel often have to solve the problem of compressing a long book into a few actors, so it may be worth a read if you want ideas on how to present Pip's narration, or Miss Havisham's house, to a class.

For Twelfth Night, also on the twenty twenty-seven list, two notices. Cornell's theatre department is staging it, and Ithaca Times describes it as a Shakespearean romantic comedy. And BroadwayWorld announces Ellyn Heald's Twelfth Night: 1941, which will have its world premiere at the Episcopal Actors' Guild in New York. No date is given, and I don't know how the nineteen forty-one setting is used, but moving the play to that year is an intriguing choice, and could prompt a good class discussion on what a historical setting adds to a comedy about disguise and longing.

Now for Atwood, who is on your oral list for The Handmaid's Tale. The Toronto Star reports that Margaret Atwood has thousands of microplastics in her blood, and that she isn't happy about it. I only have the headline, so I don't know the context. Separately, Secret Miami says she'll be among some five hundred authors at what it calls the nation's longest-running literary festival, in Miami this November, alongside Colson Whitehead and Tony Shalhoub. The details are brief, but if you like to show pupils that the authors they study are living, speaking people, an Atwood appearance is a nice thing to mention.

Finally, a few items a little to one side of the syllabus. Place Gre'net has an archive page on the Cité scolaire internationale in Grenoble. I only have the title, so I can't say what it covers, but if it holds local reporting on the school it might be worth a browse for context on international sections in the city.

On the reading side, Julia Otero, writing on RUSSPAIN.com, recommends Ousman Umar's memoir about migration. bfi.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's a Hamlet-heavy couple of days in the theatre pages, with a few other programme titles and authors drifting through, and I should say at the outset that many of these pieces reached me as little more than headlines, so I'll be careful not to pretend to know more than I do.

Let me begin with Hamlet, since it dominates. Seven items touch on it, which tells you something about how alive the play remains going into the twenty twenty-seven session.

The one with the most to chew on is The Guardian's review of a new production, which it calls extraordinary. The headline says it turns Shakespeare inside out with infinite jest, and with cuddly toys. I only have that headline and the framing, not the review itself, so I can't tell you who directs it or how the toys are used. But "infinite jest" is Hamlet's own phrase, from the graveyard, when he holds Yorick's skull and remembers a man who once carried him on his back. A production that fills the stage with soft toys seems to be playing with exactly that edge between childhood tenderness and death. That could be a lovely way into the graveyard scene with première, if the review turns out to explain the choice. It's worth reading in full when you have a quiet moment.

Also in London, Country and Town House has a stage note on Hamlet: Hail to the Thief at the Barbican. Again, only the headline reached me, so I can't say what the production does. The title itself is suggestive, though, since the thief in the play is of course Claudius, who has taken a crown, a wife and a brother's life. If you're thinking about how pupils read usurpation and legitimacy in the play, a title like that at least shows how a contemporary company chooses to frame it.

Then there's the screen. The Hindu reviews a new Hamlet film starring Riz Ahmed, under the headline that he finds method in this madness. That is a nod to Polonius, who remarks that there is method in Hamlet's apparent madness, and it points to the question every class eventually asks: is he really mad, or performing? I haven't got the review's detail, so I can't tell you whether Ahmed leans one way or the other. But a film Hamlet is useful for a different reason from a stage one, because close-ups change how soliloquies work, and that's a comparison pupils tend to enjoy making. The Hindu is also a reminder of how the play travels, read and judged well beyond Britain.

Further afield, there's a production at the Nevada Theatre, presented by TheUnion.com as a Hamlet for our time, running through the eighth of November. That's obviously not one for a weekend jaunt from Les Adrets, but the phrase is useful in itself. "A Hamlet for our time" is the claim every new production makes, and it could make a good discussion prompt with première: what would it mean for this play to speak to now, and what do we lose if we insist on it?

BroadwayWorld also has a notice that Thinking Cap Theatre is presenting Hamlet. There are no dates or details in what I have, so I'll simply note it as another sign that the play is on stages everywhere this season.

On the more reflective side, the University of Utah has a piece asking why Hamlet still matters. I have only the title, but it's exactly the question a seconde class might be asked at the start of a unit, before they've decided the answer is "because it's on the programme." If the piece is accessible, it could serve as a short stimulus text, though I'd read it first before promising anything.

And the most unusual of the lot comes from Starburst Magazine, which interviews Dan Sturman and R.C. Staab about Space Hamlet, a science-fiction reworking of the play. The extract is thin, so I can't say how faithful it is. But the idea is a good one for teaching: what survives when you move the story to space? The ghost, the revenge, the doubt, the play within the play. Asking pupils what they would keep and what they would cut in a reimagining is a neat way into the question of what the play is really made of, and it suits those who come to Shakespeare more easily through science fiction.

Now to the other titles on the twenty twenty-seven list, where there are three items.

The first is a review on southlondon.co.uk of Great Expectations at the Brockley Jack Studio in London. I only have the title, so the staging details are unknown. But Dickens on a studio stage raises a nice practical question, which is how you put a first-person retrospective narrator, and a novel with so much weather, marsh and fog, into a small room. Pip looking back at himself is a narrator's problem as much as a plot, and adaptations show how directors solve it. If the review mentions how the production handles the older Pip's voice, that would be worth passing on to première.

The second is from Ithaca Times, reporting that Cornell's theatre department is staging Twelfth Night, which they describe as a Shakespearean romantic comedy. A university production is a reminder that the play remains a staple for student companies, partly because of its gender play, disguise and music. I have no further detail, but it's a good one to keep in mind if you want to talk about how young actors approach Viola and Orsino.

The third is a BroadwayWorld notice about Ellyn Heald's Twelfth Night: 1941, which will have its world premiere at the Episcopal Actors' Guild in New York. There's no date in what I have, so only the place is certain. The setting in nineteen forty-one is intriguing, since it relocates the play to a particular historical moment, in the middle of the Second World War. I can't tell you how the adaptation uses it, but the idea of moving Illyria into wartime might interest pupils who like to link a text with its historical frame, which I know is a habit of yours.

Two items concern authors from the oral list, both involving Margaret Atwood, whose The Handmaid's Tale is among the oral themes.

Secret Miami reports that Atwood will be among some five hundred authors at the nation's longest-running literary festival, in Miami this November, alongside Colson Whitehead and Tony Shalhoub. The text is brief, so I can't say when or where she appears, nor in what format. But if recordings or interviews emerge from the festival, an Atwood conversation would be a gift for oral preparation, especially hearing an author talk about the book that pupils may be studying.

Separately, the Toronto Star reports that Atwood has thousands of microplastics in her blood and is not happy about it. I only have the headline, so I can't say how she responded or what the context was. It's more of a curiosity than a teaching resource, though there's something fitting about the author of dystopian fiction being measured, quite literally, against the contaminated world.

Finally, a few items that sit outside the programme but may interest you.

Place Gre'net has a page in its archives on the Cité scolaire internationale, the school where you teach. All I have is the title, so I can't tell you what the coverage includes. It may offer a bit of local context on the school, and since it's an archive page, there may be older material worth a browse.

The Economist has an article explaining the popularity of Max Richter's compositions. The argument isn't in what I have, but given your love of classical and contemporary music, it might be a pleasant read. Richter's work is often described as calm, spacious, and strongly tied to other arts, and I'd keep an eye out for whether the piece mentions the music's use alongside literature or dance. That's my speculation rather than anything the article says, so take it lightly.

And on RUSSPAIN.com, Julia Otero recommends Ousman Umar's memoir about migration. The book isn't described in what I have. But a first-person account of migration is the sort of narrator-driven writing you tend to enjoy, and it could sit well alongside the voices in Brick Lane, which is on the twenty twenty-seven list, if you wanted a non-fiction companion. Again, that's a possible link, not something the item claims.

So, in short, it's a good moment for Hamlet, with the Guardian review the one most worth reading in full, and a handful of smaller hints for Dickens, Shakespeare's comedy and Atwood. Enjoy a quiet cup of something warm and the first frosty light on Belledonne.

Good morning, Yamuna. It's Friday the sixth of November, and the last couple of days have left a pleasing spread of local evenings, a village celebration and some theatre to plan around, so let me take you through it by theme.

Let me start with tonight, because Friday the sixth is unusually busy in the Grésivaudan, and there's a lot of choice for a single evening.

For someone who loves a strong narrative voice, the one I'd point to first is Contes Shipibos, by Compagnie Caminos. It's at Espace Aragon in Villard-Bonnot, starting at seven this evening. It's an evening of oral storytelling, tales told aloud in the Shipibo tradition. There's something special about stories that exist first as a voice in a room, before they are ever words on a page, and since you spend your days with narrators and how they hold a reader, this could be a lovely one to simply sit inside. You don't need to know anything about the culture beforehand. The listing gives no more detail than that, but the format promises exactly the kind of story you can step into.

Then there's Pontcharra, where two things are happening tonight. The first is a concert called Autour d'Anne Sylvestre, a programme built around the songs of Anne Sylvestre. It runs from eight o'clock to twenty past nine. Her songs are French chanson with a real literary streak, with words that matter as much as the tune, so it sits very comfortably alongside your taste for language that has music in it. It's a fairly compact evening too, just over an hour and twenty minutes, which is pleasant on a Friday night when the week has been long.

The second Pontcharra event is a performance called AMOURS, by Cie Muchmuche Company, part of the Saison Echos season. I should be honest: the listing doesn't say what form it takes or what it's about, and it gives no start time in what I have. So I can tell you it exists and where it is, but you'd want to look up the details before heading out. The title alone suggests something worth being curious about.

And a third option, a little further up the valley's side: the Péninsule Trio are playing at the Salle des fêtes Dupanloup in La Combe-de-Lancey, also tonight. Again, the listing doesn't tell us the programme or the genre, nor the time. A village hall, a trio, a Friday evening in November: it sounds intimate, and these small concerts can turn out to be the best ones, but it's one to check before you commit.

So that's four possibilities for tonight. The Villard-Bonnot tales start at seven and the Pontcharra concert at eight, so realistically you'd choose between them rather than do both. My own instinct, knowing you, would be the storytelling if you want to be transported, and the Anne Sylvestre evening if you'd rather have words and melody together.

Moving on to the weekend, which runs from today through Sunday the eighth. The jds.fr site has put together a round-up for Isère covering the sixth to the eighth of November, with concerts, shows, the Foire de Grenoble and some more unusual activities. The Foire de Grenoble gets a mention there as one of the big weekend draws.

If you like to catch a venue early in its season and pick out a concert or a performance for the weeks ahead, this is a natural time to do so.

The article, at least as I have it, doesn't give dates, so I can't tell you when it falls, but since it's in your own village, it will probably be easy to spot on a noticeboard or hear about from a neighbour. A fête like this, in a village at the foot of Belledonne, in autumn light, is the kind of local life that seems made for a slow walk with no particular schedule.

Now, music of a different kind. In Eybens, just by Grenoble, there's a baroque concert titled Venise au temps de Vivaldi, Venice in the time of Vivaldi. If you find the date, it might be a good one.

Then in Meylan, the Théâtre Hexagone, the Scène nationale, has a clutch of things coming up, and I'll take them in date order.

It follows a child confined to night, and it deals with the need to speak out about incest. That is a heavy subject, and I want to say so plainly. It's serious theatre, aimed at young audiences as well as adults, and it might be something you'd think about in connection with your own work, or simply as a piece that treats a difficult subject with care. It may not be one for a light night out, but it sounds like theatre that matters.

On the other side of the tonal scale, on Wednesday the twenty-fifth of November at half past seven in the evening, comes Le Poids des choses, a circus and illusion show by Camille Boitel. It's for ages seven and up and lasts about forty-five minutes, with two more dates listed. It plays with gravity, with the weight of objects and bodies, and it sounds physical and playful. Since you enjoy dance, the way movement tells a story without words might be right up your street. It's also short, which makes it an easy midweek treat.

It's a one-hour sound installation and performance exploring time, rhythm and listening, with three further dates listed. For anyone who likes close attention to language and form, and to music as something you really listen to rather than just hear, this one sounds intriguing. Time, rhythm and listening are, after all, as much the stuff of poetry as of sound.

And looking further ahead, the Hexagone has announced that the thirteenth EXPERIMENTA biennial will come in twenty twenty-seven, under the name EXPERIMENTA slash PERFORMA. No dates yet, but it promises eighty proposals of exhibitions, shows and performances, with twenty-three partners across the territory. That's a big, wide-ranging programme, and it's good to know about early. It's one to keep at the back of your mind for next year, especially if you like it when art spills out of theatres and into the places around you.

For something visual, there's an exhibition in Crolles. Brayogrammes is a photography exhibition by Cédric Poulain, running from the fourth of November to the fourth of December, and entry is free. A month is a generous window, so there's no pressure to go this weekend. It's the sort of thing you can fit around a market morning or a trip down the valley, and free entry makes it easy to pop in without any commitment. The listing doesn't say more about the subject of the images, so you'd go with an open eye, which is sometimes the best way to see photographs.

And one last item, from Grenoble. The Dolce Cinema festival is celebrating its twentieth edition, dedicated to Italian cinema. The date isn't given in what I have. I mention it briefly, knowing that cinema news isn't usually your priority, but twenty years of a festival devoted to one country's films is a fine thing, and Italian cinema has such a tradition of strong storytelling that it may tempt you if you have a free evening in Grenoble.

So, to sum up the practical bits. Tonight, you have storytelling in Villard-Bonnot at seven, and songs of Anne Sylvestre in Pontcharra at eight, with AMOURS and the Péninsule Trio as less well described alternatives. Tomorrow, Saint-Maximin opens its season. Over the weekend there's the Foire de Grenoble. Through to early December, the Crolles photographs are there for the looking. And after that, a rich run of theatre in Meylan through late November and early December.

Whatever you choose, I hope there's a good story or a good song waiting for you somewhere this weekend.

Good morning, Yamuna. Today's good news has a lot of stories in it, and a good few of them end better than they began.

Let me start with books and the tales behind them. The Guardian reports that China Miéville has won the ten thousand pound Goldsmiths prize for The Rouse. It runs to twelve hundred and sixty-four pages, part paranormal thriller and part historical saga, moving through British imperial and Cold War history. It took him twenty years to write, and the judges called it exuberant and overflowing. One of them said he was destined for this award. It may be one for your shelves, or at least for a very sturdy bookmark.

Staying with stories, Upworthy retells how H. A. and Margret Rey, the couple behind Curious George, escaped the Nazis on bicycles during the Second World War, carrying their original manuscripts with them. It is a lovely reminder that a little mischievous monkey came out of a real flight for safety, and that the pages survived because two people refused to leave them behind. And at the Château de Chantilly, Beaux Arts Magazine says the pink diamond is being explored through its strange destiny. Stolen in nineteen twenty-six, later recovered, and wrapped in legend ever since, it has the shape of a novel already. The magazine calls it a miraculé, a jewel that somehow survived. If you fancy a day out, it could be worth keeping an eye on what Chantilly does with it.

There is also a gentler kind of mystery. Good News Network describes a short documentary from JoyDrops, in which the filmmaker Ora DeKornfeld pieces together the hidden family history of her grandfather, a man who would never talk about it, after he turned ninety-nine. A buried past, a patient granddaughter, and a story finally told. And for something closer to a thriller, scientists have used an ordinary hospital CT scanner to read a four-hundred-year-old padlock, found in a treasure-laden shipwreck on a Welsh beach. The puzzle had resisted solving for more than twenty years, and a scan, without forcing or breaking anything, did it.

Now to music and dance. Good News Network's history column notes that on the fifth of November, nineteen fifty-five, the Vienna State Opera reopened after being destroyed in the Second World War. It is a house tied to Mahler and to the Vienna Philharmonic, so it feels fitting to remember it being rebuilt and singing again. In dance, The Guardian has an interview with the Greek choreographer Christos Papadopoulos, who has won the first Rose international prize for choreography, already nicknamed the Turner prize for dance. It was awarded for his piece Larsen C. He talks candidly about failure, friction, and asking the near-impossible of his dancers, which makes for a thoughtful read. And if you would like something to watch, ARTE Regards has a thirty-minute reportage from Rome, available until twenty thirty-one. It visits a seniors' centre in Trastevere that serves more than two thousand retirees with painting and dance classes, shared meals and plenty of solidarity. It sounds like an hour of sunshine, even in November.

On history, Good News Network marks eight hundred and nine years since King Henry the Third signed the Charter of the Forest. It was a law that gave free men the right to use forests once reserved for the crown. It is a companion piece to the Magna Carta story, and an easy way to bring a quieter, very practical sort of liberty into a classroom discussion.

For nature, there are three encouraging items. Brazil has enlarged Pantanal Matogrossense National Park by about one hundred and eighty-five square miles, which is more than a quarter of its original size. The wetland is described as one of the richest and most sensitive biomes on the planet. On England's south coast, Good News Network reports that sandwich terns have returned to a colony that avian flu wiped out three years ago. The count has gone from zero to seven hundred and fifty-six birds, and the conservation work has also helped little terns, ringed plovers, gulls and oystercatchers recover. And for the sky, the Northern Taurid meteor shower is due to peak a few days after Monday the ninth of November, when the New Moon should leave the sky at its darkest. The Taurids are known for their long, luminous tails, so if the clouds over Belledonne are kind, a few minutes outdoors after dark could be rewarded.

Finally, some human stories of courage and care. Reasons to be Cheerful visits Erik's Ranch and Retreats, near Livingston in Montana. It is a guest retreat on two hundred and thirty acres of pasture and wilderness, where autistic people work as concierges, guides, wranglers and cooks. The whole place is built around its staff, which gives the work a real sense of dignity. In health, The Optimist Daily reports that a personalised brain therapy called Magnetic e-Resonance Therapy has been cleared by the American FDA for post-traumatic stress disorder. In clinical trials it reported sixty-eight per cent remission, compared with about ten point nine per cent for the best approved medications, which would be a remarkable difference if it holds up in wider use. And in sport, the long-distance swimmer Catherine Breed has become the first person to swim the entire California coastline. It took her about nine hundred miles and a hundred and eleven days, through extreme weather, hard currents and eight shark encounters.

That is all for today, and I hope something here gives you a smile with your coffee.

Good morning, Yamuna. The last two days have brought a rather generous pile of good news, with a lot in it for a reader and a lover of music, so let me start with the stories.

The big literary news comes from The Guardian. China Miéville has won the Goldsmiths prize, worth ten thousand pounds, for a novel called The Rouse. It runs to one thousand, two hundred and sixty-four pages, and it blends a paranormal thriller with a historical saga that moves through British imperial history and into the Cold War. It took him about twenty years to write. The judges called it exuberant and overflowing, and one of them said he was destined for this award. I rather like the idea of a book that big winning a prize that is all about daring in fiction. Whether or not you ever carry it home, it is a lovely thing to mention to a sixth-former who thinks a novel of three hundred pages is already too much.

Staying with books, Upworthy tells the story of H. A. and Margret Rey, the couple who created Curious George. During the Second World War they escaped the Nazis on bicycles, and they carried their original manuscripts with them. It is a small, vivid image: two people pedalling away from catastrophe with a monkey's adventures in their luggage. It is the sort of history that a pupil can step into without any background, and the story ends on a hopeful note, which is more than can be said for many wartime tales. If you ever want to introduce a class to the idea that stories are worth saving, it is a gentle way in.

There is also something with the shape of a novel from the Château de Chantilly. Beaux Arts Magazine reports that the château is exploring the history of its pink diamond, described as a miracle survivor. The stone was stolen in nineteen twenty-six, later recovered, and has been wrapped in legend ever since. Theft, disappearance, rediscovery and mystery: it has all the ingredients of a good thriller, and the magazine's piece is worth a read for the atmosphere alone.

And a more intimate story of buried pasts. Good News Network features a short documentary from the JoyDrops series, The Grandfather Puzzle. The filmmaker, Ora DeKornfeld, pieces together a family history that her grandfather would never talk about, and she begins the work after he turns ninety-nine. A man who has kept silent for nearly a century, and a granddaughter patient enough to put the pieces together. It has the narrative pull of a memoir, and it is a reminder that the quiet people in a family are often the ones with the largest stories.

Along the same lines, history of a gentler sort. The Good News in History column marks eight hundred and nine years since King Henry the Third signed the Charter of the Forest in England. It was a law granting free men the right to use forests that had once been reserved for the crown. It sits alongside the Magna Carta story, but it is the more earthly of the two, concerned with firewood, pasture and the everyday business of living. It might make a surprising companion piece if you are ever teaching texts in which forests carry meaning, as they so often do in English literature.

Now to music and dance. The Guardian has an interview with the Greek choreographer Christos Papadopoulos, who has won the first Rose international prize for choreography, which the paper describes as the Turner prize for dance. He won it for a piece called Larsen C. In the interview he talks about failure, about friction, and about asking the near-impossible of his dancers, and also about what the prize money means to him. There is something disarming about a prizewinner who chooses to talk about failure first. If you enjoy dance documentaries, the way he describes the work in the studio will probably appeal.

On the classical side, the Good News in History column for the fifth of November remembers that on that date in nineteen fifty-five the Vienna State Opera reopened, after being destroyed in the Second World War. The note links the house to Mahler and to the Vienna Philharmonic. It is an uplifting anniversary: a great opera house rebuilt and the music resuming, a decade after the war ended.

And a piece of television that brings dance and community together. ARTE Regards has a thirty-minute reportage, Rome: retraités, mais toujours actifs, available until twenty thirty-one, so there is no hurry. It takes us to a seniors' centre in Trastevere that serves more than two thousand retirees. They paint, they dance, they share meals, and they look after one another. It sounds like the kind of film you could put on after a long week and come away from feeling a little lighter, and perhaps a little more hopeful about growing older.

On to the human stories, and one in particular that I found rather moving. Reasons to be Cheerful visits Erik's Ranch and Retreats, near Livingston in Montana. It is a guest retreat on two hundred and thirty acres of pasture and wilderness, and autistic people work there as concierges, guides, wranglers and cooks. The point is that the place has been built around its staff rather than asking staff to fit around a place. It is a story about work and dignity, and about what happens when an employer starts with people's strengths. I think it would speak to anyone who has watched a pupil struggle in a setting that was not designed for them.

In health, The Optimist Daily reports that a personalised brain therapy called Magnetic e-Resonance Therapy has been cleared by the American regulator, the FDA, for post-traumatic stress disorder. The reported figure from clinical trials is sixty-eight per cent remission, and the piece compares that with about ten point nine per cent for the best approved medications. As always with figures like these, it is worth remembering that they come from the trials and as reported by the outlet, but they are striking, and for people living with PTSD any new route to recovery is welcome news.

Now for a thriller of a more practical kind. Good News Network reports that a four-hundred-year-old padlock, found in a treasure-laden shipwreck on a Welsh beach, has finally given up its secret. For more than twenty years nobody could work out how it functioned. Scientists have now read it using a hospital CT scanner, the same machine that looks inside people, and the puzzle is solved. I like the idea of a medical scan turning into a key, and of a mystery that lasted over two decades being cracked by borrowing time on equipment that was sitting in a hospital. It would not be out of place at the start of a detective novel.

Let me turn to nature, where there is plenty of encouragement. In Brazil, Pantanal Matogrossense National Park has been enlarged by about one hundred and eighty-five square miles, which is more than a quarter of its original size. The Pantanal is described as one of the richest and most sensitive biomes on the planet, a vast wetland, and extending the protection is a concrete outcome rather than a promise.

Closer to home, and rather more cheering still, Sandwich terns have returned to a colony on England's south coast three years after avian flu wiped it out. The colony has gone from zero birds to seven hundred and fifty-six. Conservation work also helped little terns, ringed plovers, gulls and oystercatchers to recover. Zero to seven hundred and fifty-six is the sort of number that makes one want to go and stand on a beach and listen. It is a reminder that a disaster is not always the end of the story, particularly when people keep up the patient work of protection.

And for a human triumph in the water, Good News Network reports that Catherine Breed has become the first person to swim the entire California coastline. It was about nine hundred miles, over one hundred and eleven days. Along the way she met extreme weather, hard currents, and eight encounters with sharks. I would not enjoy a single one of those days, but I admire her stamina enormously, and it is a lovely example of what sustained, stubborn effort can achieve.

Finally, something you can enjoy for free, and from your doorstep in Les Adrets, where the dark skies of Belledonne ought to help. Good News Network notes that the Northern Taurid meteor shower is due to peak a few days after Monday the ninth of November. That is when the new moon should make the sky darkest, so the long, luminous tails of the meteors should show up well. The advice is simply to find somewhere away from lights, wrap up warmly, give your eyes time to adjust, and look up. A flask of something hot would be sensible. The meteors are famously unhurried, with those long, glowing tails, so it should be an appealingly gentle show.

If I had to pick a thread through today's stories, it would be people carrying something precious through difficult times: manuscripts on bicycles, a family secret across ninety-nine years, a colony of seabirds back from nothing. Go well today, and I hope the sky is clear for the meteors.

Every lost week in a lycée is a week of teaching that has to be fitted in somewhere else, and the exam calendar does not move.

Their message was that they are working under strain, and that they are facing violence of what they describe as unprecedented gravity. One of the headlines quotes them as saying that, whatever they do, they are caught in a vice, and that the situation could explode on any given day. Those are strong words from people who are not usually given to drama. All of this comes against the background of the continuing student protests, and the heads are describing a job in which they are squeezed between pupils, parents, staff and the authorities, with very little room to manoeuvre.

The wider picture is that the school protests are now part of something larger. The Guardian reports that France is bracing for a day of strike action, with hundreds of thousands of people expected to join nationwide marches and strikes. Hospital staff, rail workers and air traffic staff are joining teachers and students, who are protesting about poor teaching conditions. The Guardian's piece is mostly concerned with the cost of living and labour unrest, so I will not dwell on that side of it, but it is worth knowing that on a strike day you should expect disruption to trains and flights, so if you have any journey planned, it is wise to check before you set out.

There is one more education story, this time looking further ahead, which may be useful background for your première and terminale students. Franceinfo reports on the announced end of Parcoursup, the national platform through which pupils apply to university. The announcement has opened up a debate that has never quite gone away: should universities be allowed to select their students, or should anyone with the baccalauréat be admitted without sorting? Franceinfo frames it as a choice between what it calls an openly acknowledged selection and a total absence of sorting. The question is becoming more pressing because the number of baccalauréat holders keeps rising, so there are more candidates every year for the same places. It is the sort of thing your older pupils may well have opinions about, since they are the ones who will live with whatever replaces it.

Now to the weather, which is rather wet in the south. The Local France reports that two départements in southern France were placed on orange alert for heavy rain and flooding, with warnings in force from ten o'clock on Thursday morning. Separately, franceinfo says that both Corsican départements are on orange alert for rain and flooding, with more than two hundred millimetres of rain expected on the eastern side of the island. Neither is likely to affect life in Les Adrets, but if you have friends or plans in the south, a quick check of the forecast would be sensible.

On travel, there is a small piece of encouraging news for anyone who likes to cross the Channel with a pet. The Local France says that an agreement between the European Union and the United Kingdom, expected at the upcoming summit, could bring back pet passports. That would make journeys easier for holidaymakers travelling with dogs, cats and, rather charmingly, ferrets. I should be clear that the deal has not yet been announced, so for now this is a prospect, not a settled change. Still, if you or colleagues in the British section ever travel with an animal, it is one to keep an eye on.

There was also a rather odd disruption in the skies on Thursday. The Guardian reported, in a live account, that a Dublin to Rome flight landed at a French military base after one of several bomb threats made against commercial flights across Europe. Threats were also reported in Italy, Czechia, Bulgaria and Belgium, and several planes were diverted. The threats were later found to be hoaxes, so nobody was harmed, and I mention it only so that you are not alarmed if you see the headline.

Now for something gentler, and I suspect more to your taste: a little cluster of pieces about language. The Local France has been in a playful mood this week. The first is the weekly La Belle Vie column, which explores some of the complexities of the French language alongside a declared love for cheese. It is a short text, but a pleasant one, and you can imagine that those two subjects sit rather comfortably together, since both are things that foreigners find baffling and French people find entirely natural.

The second is a light piece on what the French call gentilés, the names given to the people who live in particular towns. Some of them are, apparently, surprisingly hard to guess. Anyone who has tried to work out what to call the inhabitants of a town they have never visited will know the feeling. There is a certain poetry in it, and a good deal of local colour. For a Grenoble-area reader, it is a nice reminder that every valley and every village carries its own small vocabulary of belonging.

The third is the Local's French Expression of the Day, which is faire amende honorable. The piece points out that, despite appearances, it has nothing to do with the word amende meaning a fine. It means, in essence, to make a public apology or to make amends, and it is one of those expressions where the English reader's instinct leads you cheerfully astray. It could make a tidy little example for a class on false friends, or on how phrases carry old meanings inside them long after we have stopped noticing.

The Local France also has a podcast this week, and it is a mixed bag. It covers the latest on French protests, including a warning about tear gas, and a possible easing of doctor's appointments in rural France. The segment most likely to catch your ear, I think, is the one asking which city locals consider to speak the most perfect French. Anyone who has spent time in France knows that this is a question guaranteed to start an argument at the dinner table, and I would guess that everyone has a confident and slightly different answer.

Turning to history, there is a lovely archive piece from the Guardian that suits a reader who likes to learn the past through writing from the time. It looks back at how the paper reported the Suez crisis of nineteen fifty-six, after Nasser nationalised the canal and Britain, France and Israel attacked. The headline phrase is "wrong on every count", which is the verdict of hindsight on the paper's own coverage. What makes it interesting is that it shows history as it was written while it was happening, with all the confidence, blind spots and misjudgements that implies. It is a neat lesson in how a narrator can be sure of himself and still be mistaken, which is a theme you could carry from newspaper columns straight into the unreliable narrators of fiction.

Closely related, though from a different angle, is an analysis from the Local France asking why so many of France's most successful films of twenty twenty-six are set during the Second World War. The piece wonders whether this reflects modern anxieties, as if audiences are reaching back to that period to think about the present. The angle is largely about cinema and its audiences, which I know is not your main interest, but the underlying question is a good literary one: why do certain periods return again and again in fiction, and what do they let us say about our own time that we cannot say directly?

briefing.text:
Good morning, Yamuna, and happy Friday. Here is your Daily Yam for the sixth of November.

Let's begin with books, because it's a good day for them. The Guardian marks the centenary of John Berger with a "where to start" guide to his work, which moves freely between art, love, mortality and more. If you've ever wanted to know where to enter Berger, this is a gentle map, and his writing on painting and on seeing sits very close to your own interests.

Also from the Guardian, an interview with the Indian-Irish poet Nikita Gill. She talks about her earliest reading memories, at sea with her sailor father, and about the retelling of the Mahabharata that first made her want to write. She also speaks of her admiration for Arundhati Roy and Lucille Clifton. The headline gives away a lovely confession: she read Flowers in the Attic far too young, and says someone should have stopped her.

For prizes, a reviewer at The i Paper says they have read every novel on this year's Booker shortlist and believe there is a clear winner. It's a close reading of the whole list, so it may help you decide where to place your own bet.

Two pieces for the ear, too. Literary Hub prints Mahmoud Darwish's poem "Arabic Music" in full, with its quiet, meditative questions about stones, clouds and sparrows. It's the sort of poem that asks to be read aloud. And Literary Hub also has an excerpt from a short fiction piece called "Dams", in which a woman named Ada, over coffee, notices the translucence of two words, the Catalan escriure, to write, and novel·la, as she explains why she has come back. It's a small moment of real attention to language.

Now to art, and to the places where words and images meet. At the Bibliothèque nationale de France in Paris, an exhibition celebrates the obsessions of Georges Perec, drawing on more than forty years of his work across literature and the visual arts. Beaux Arts Magazine calls it abundant and wide-ranging. If you find yourself in Paris, it sounds well worth a detour.

Closer to home, there's a guided tour tomorrow, Saturday the seventh of November, at half past four at the Musée de Grenoble. It looks at the François Morellet display, called "Under the geometry, the mischief". Morellet's playful geometric abstraction makes a cheerful way into the museum on a November afternoon.

On to your BFI corner, and two takes on Hamlet, which is on the 2027 programme. The Guardian reviews a new stage production that, in its words, turns Shakespeare inside out, with infinite jest and cuddly toys. That might give your seconde or première classes a very different angle on the play. And The Hindu reviews a new Hamlet film starring Riz Ahmed, under the headline that he finds method in this madness. Put side by side, the two reviews show how differently the play is being staged and adapted at the moment, which could be a useful conversation to have in class.

Now some things close to Les Adrets. At the Théâtre Hexagone in Meylan, on the third of December at six in the evening, Clément Edouard presents "Hypertemps", a one-hour sound installation and performance about time, rhythm and listening. There are three further dates if that evening doesn't suit. And in Eybens, there's a baroque concert called "Venice at the Time of Vivaldi". The listing doesn't give a date, so it's worth checking with the organisers before you plan anything, but it sounds just right for you.

For viewing, ARTE has two programmes. The first is "L'écrivain et l'assassin", in which Emmanuel Carrère revisits the difficult writing of L'Adversaire, his book about Jean-Claude Romand, who killed his family in 1993 after years of lies. It's available until the third of March next year, and it shows how a true crime became a novel, which is something you could happily use in class. The second is a lighter watch: an ARTE Regards report from Rome, thirty minutes long, set in a seniors' centre in Trastevere that serves more than two thousand retirees with painting and dance classes, shared meals and plenty of solidarity. It's available until twenty thirty-one, so there's no rush.

Now for the good news. Reasons to be Cheerful visits Erik's Ranch and Retreats, near Livingston in Montana, a guest retreat on two hundred and thirty acres of pasture and wilderness. Autistic people work there as concierges, guides, wranglers and cooks, and the whole place is built around its staff. It's a warm story about work and dignity.

And here is a puzzle with a thriller's feel. Good News Network reports that scientists have used a hospital CT scanner to read a four-hundred-year-old padlock, found in a treasure-laden shipwreck on a Welsh beach. The mystery had lasted more than twenty years, and it is now solved.

Finally, two light reads from The Local France. This week's La Belle Vie column looks at the quirks of the French language and at favourite French cheeses. It's brief, but it will make you smile. The other is about the "gentilés", the names given to people who live in French towns, some of which are surprisingly hard to guess. It might even be fun to test your pupils on a few from around Grenoble.

That's everything for today, Yamuna. I hope your morning is gentle, and that something beautiful finds you before the weekend.
